clue.text: Neighbourhood scruff coming from teddy bears' picnic area

blocks.note: the scruff is the back of the neck
'of' can mean coming from, as in 'a man of Kent'
the song begins 'If you go down to the woods today', where the teddy bears have their picnic

explanation.surface: Someone scruffy seems to have wandered in from the woods where the teddy bears picnic.
explanation.definitionFit: Your neck of the woods is an idiom for the area where you live, your local district.

clue.text: Vehicle swamped by rain burst seen in a perfect state

indicators.note: something swamped is engulfed, so it ends up surrounded by the other letters
a burst scatters its contents, so the word's letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged
a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A car caught in a sudden downpour is somehow said to be in a state of perfection.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism, nirvana is the state of perfect peace and release from suffering.

clue.text: Member in exclusive club best incriminate for corruption?

indicators.note: corrupting something spoils its proper form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A member of a select club is best pinned with a corruption charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'exclusive club' is the Cabinet, the small group of senior government ministers in the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabinet minister belongs to the small, select body of senior government ministers, a club few can join.

clue.text: Test in cricket ground with Victor going for runs

indicators.note: one thing going in exchange for another means a letter is swapped out

blocks.note: the Oval is a Test cricket ground in south London
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A Test match at a cricket ground, with a batsman called Victor swapped for faster scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' looks like a cricket Test match, but it is the definition: an exam.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral is a spoken examination, a kind of test.

clue.text: Protector needs to step up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a pace is a single step

explanation.surface: A guardian needs to rise to the challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step up' reads as one idiom; split it into a word and a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A toecap is the reinforced front of a boot, which protects the toes.

clue.text: Sweet's taken with no starter and a come-on to see these?

indicators.note: with no starter, the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: fetching means attractive or sweet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is charmed by a sweet and an invitation to come and see something.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the old chat-up line 'Come up and see my etchings', a pretext for getting someone home.
explanation.definitionFit: Etchings are prints, famously the pretext in the seducer's line inviting someone up to view them.

clue.text: Cooked up alibi, got no charge

indicators.note: something cooked up is concocted, so these letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A suspect invented an alibi and escaped being charged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like a criminal accusation, but it is the definition in its sense of duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge can mean a duty or responsibility entrusted to someone, which is an obligation.

clue.text: Scarper! Guys emptied tills and split shop

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, the word keeps only its outer letters

blocks.note: to scarper is to run off, to leave
guys are men
first and last letters only
tore means split or ripped

explanation.surface: Robbers empty the cash registers and flee the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Scarper is British slang for run away. The robbery picture makes 'split' look like fleeing; it means ripped.
explanation.definitionFit: A department store is a large shop selling many kinds of goods in separate sections.

clue.text: Shock centrepiece of show, Three Kings receiving Oscar

indicators.note: the centrepiece is the middle, so only the central letters are kept
receiving something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside the group

blocks.note: the two central letters
R (rex) stands for king, three times
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: The Nativity play's shocking highlight: the Three Kings hand an Oscar award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Three Kings evoke the Nativity, but here they are just three Rs, with O going between the second and third.
explanation.definitionFit: Horror is intense fear or dismay, a feeling of shock.

clue.text: Kid with pen one's found in chest

blocks.note: to kid someone is to tease or rib them
a pen is an enclosure, like a cage

explanation.surface: A child with a pen has been discovered inside a chest, perhaps hiding in a toy box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a noun, a child, but works as the verb to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: The bony frame of ribs is located in the human chest, enclosing the heart and lungs.

clue.text: It's musical 'cosplay', getting dressed up

indicators.note: dressing up changes how something looks, so the word's letters are rearranged into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cosplay, where fans dress up as characters, is being described as a musical event.
explanation.walkthrough: The cosplay setting makes 'dressed up' sound literal; it is the instruction to rearrange the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Calypso is a style of Caribbean music from Trinidad, so it is something musical.

clue.text: Relative making visit, not husband

indicators.note: 'not' tells you the following item must be taken away from the word

blocks.note: to haunt a place is to visit it often
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A relation comes to stay without her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: An aunt is a family member, your parent's sister, so she is a relative.

clue.text: Me in gear with fantastic style, tying up left then right loafer

indicators.note: something styled fantastically is made over in a fanciful new arrangement
tying something up wraps it round, so the rearranged letters enclose the other items

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for left
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A fashion boast about wearing stylish gear, oddly ending in an accusation of laziness.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters become MAINGEER; L goes in after MA and R after MAINGE, in that order, giving MALINGERER.
explanation.definitionFit: A malingerer shirks work by feigning illness, so is a loafer or idler.

clue.text: Raised fences have gone down

indicators.note: a fence encloses ground, so this word surrounds the next

blocks.note: raised as in reared, brought up
to have something is to own it
food that has gone is off

explanation.surface: Fences that were put up have now collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised fences' reads as fences put up; instead the word for raised encloses the word for have. Browned off is British slang for fed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Browned off is informal British for fed up and dispirited, which is feeling down.

clue.text: Spar's produced lead-free pudding

indicators.note: free of its lead means the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: read as 'spars', the plural: roof beams

explanation.surface: The Spar convenience store has brought out a pudding with no lead in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Spar is a UK chain of corner shops, but here it is the beam, and the apostrophe-s is read as a plural. Afters is British slang for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is informal British for the course that comes after the main one: dessert, or pudding.

clue.text: Some Z-reg GTi Mercury that's got sand in the works

definitions.text: that's got sand in the works

indicators.note: 'some' means only part of the following words is taken, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: An old Z-registration Golf GTi or Mercury car has sand in its engine.
explanation.walkthrough: A Z-reg plate marks a British car from the early 1980s; sand in the works sounds like a ruined engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional egg timer is a small hourglass, with running sand as its working part.

clue.text: Risk a wet upset?

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disturbed, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Is it worth chancing a soaking spill?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: skimming over water always risks a wet tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Being towed across water on skis invites a soaking fall, so the sport is risking a wet upset.

clue.text: Clobber that's functional when it's wet

definitions.text: Clobber that's functional when it's wet

blocks.clueFragment: Clobber that's functional when it's wet
blocks.note: surface reading: clothing that still works after it gets soaked, like a raincoat
setter's reading: clothes whose whole purpose is to be worn in the water

explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is British slang for clothes or gear. The clue suggests waterproofs, but the garments meant are worn for a dip in the pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Costumes for bathing are designed to be used while wet, unlike most clothing.

clue.text: A deal of concern at lush standing for national leader

indicators.note: a deal of something is a portion of it, so only part of the following words is used
in a down entry, standing up means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: There is a lot of worry about a drunkard representing a country as its leader.
explanation.walkthrough: A lush is a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultan is the sovereign ruler of certain Muslim countries, so a leader of a nation.

clue.text: Associate hospital with old boys taking in last of oxygen

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece sits within the other
'last of' keeps only the last letter of 'oxygen'

blocks.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital
OB stands for old boy, so two of them
final letter of oxygen

explanation.surface: Someone links a hospital with ex-pupils who need oxygen.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially, especially with the well-connected: to associate with them.

clue.text: Hounds, nags, dogs, or other animals?

definitions.note: plural noun; the verb sense above is third person

blocks.note: first meaning: pesters persistently
second meaning: burrowing black-and-white mammals

explanation.walkthrough: The list of hounds and dogs suggests animals, but they are verbs meaning pesters; only the second meaning is a creature.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger someone is to pester them, and badgers are also nocturnal burrowing mammals of woodland.

clue.text: Tick's sitting on farm animal somewhere in Europe

blocks.note: a tick or mo is a moment, plus the S
a cow is a farm animal

explanation.surface: A parasitic tick is clinging to a cow somewhere on the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'sitting on' puts the first piece above the second. Tick and mo both mean a moment in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow, the Russian capital, lies in the European part of Russia.

clue.text: Face twisted of course in age, and spotted

indicators.note: twisted round, the word is turned to run the other way
'in' places one item inside the other

blocks.note: dial is slang for a face, also a clock face
an emphatic agreement
an aeon or eon is a long age

explanation.surface: A face has become contorted, naturally, as the years passed and it got spotty.
explanation.definitionFit: To have laid eyes on something is an idiom for having seen or noticed it.

clue.text: American edition, not new

blocks.note: abbreviation for American, as in US
abbreviation for edition

explanation.surface: A US edition of a book being sold second-hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Used goods are second-hand, previously owned, so not new.

clue.text: Mark's second Jag?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a Jaguar, informally Jag, is a car

explanation.surface: A man called Mark owns a second Jaguar.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a name; it is the definition, a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a mark left on the skin after a wound has healed.

clue.text: Creators cause sides to split describing comic hero

indicators.note: with its sides leaving, the word keeps only its inner letters
to describe a shape is to draw round it, so these letters surround the next item

blocks.note: the inner letters, with first and last dropped
the Norse god is a Marvel comic-book hero

explanation.surface: Writers cause a political split by portraying a comic-book hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sides' tempts as political factions, but it means the end letters of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Authors are writers, the people who create books and stories, and more generally originators of anything.

clue.text: Ride carries on in storm

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so this word holds the next inside

blocks.note: to ride a bike is to cycle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cyclist keeps going through a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carries on' reads as one phrase meaning continues; split it into a containment signal and the word on.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyclone is a violent storm with winds rotating around a low-pressure centre.

clue.text: They distribute pricey tickets for show on screen

definitions.text: They distribute pricey tickets for show on screen

blocks.clueFragment: They distribute pricey tickets for show on screen
blocks.note: surface reading: ticket sellers charging a lot for a film or TV show

blocks.clueFragment: pricey tickets for show on screen
blocks.note: setter's reading: officials who hand out expensive parking fines, put on display on the car windscreen

explanation.walkthrough: The 'show on screen' is not a film: the parking ticket is stuck on the windscreen for all to see. Traffic wardens are British parking enforcement officers.
explanation.definitionFit: These officers issue costly penalty notices to illegally parked cars, placing them on the windscreen.
